The blonde ray (Raja brachyura) is a relatively large skate species inhabiting continental shelf waters of the eastern North Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, with life-history traits reflecting a slow-paced demography typical of many elasmobranchs. Neonates emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 17 cm [Lb = 17 cm], a size that provides a degree of refuge from gape-limited predators while still necessitating rapid early growth to reduce vulnerability. The species is known to attain a considerable ultimate total length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], ranking it among the larger members of the Rajidae in its range. Studies conducted in captivity under controlled thermal conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] indicate that the incubation period for the fertilised ovum is roughly 213 days, which corresponds to an age at birth of approximately 213 days [ab = approximately 213 days], an extended developmental duration that aligns with the low metabolic rates and high yolk investment characteristic of oviparous skates. Egg cases are often deposited on soft sediment habitats where they remain exposed to ambient water temperatures.

Reproductive output in the blonde ray has been quantified in several fisheries-independent surveys and captive holding studies, providing insight into the species' relatively low fecundity. Females produce egg cases individually over an extended laying period, with each egg case containing a single embryo, resulting in a per-event fecundity of 1 egg per egg case [N_R_i = 1 egg per egg case]. At a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the laying frequency reaches approximately 30 egg cases per year [Ri = approximately 30 egg cases per year], a modest annual production that reflects the energetic constraints of producing large, robust egg cases. This yields a daily reproduction rate of 30 eggs per year [Ri = 30 eggs per year]. Such a strategy is typical of many rajiform skates, where iteroparity and low annual fecundity are balanced by high neonatal survival afforded by the protective egg case and substantial yolk reserves that support the embryo through a prolonged developmental period before the onset of exogenous feeding.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult blonde rays has been recorded as 7,865 grams [Wwi = 7,865 grams] in comprehensive growth studies, though some exceptionally large individuals documented in fishery landings have exceeded 14 kilograms, suggesting that asymptotic mass may vary regionally with prey availability and habitat quality. This body mass, combined with the species' ultimate total length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], yields a relatively robust body shape typical of demersal skates that forage on benthic invertebrates and small fishes. Growth parameters derived from vertebral banding patterns indicate that females tend to reach larger asymptotic sizes than males, a common pattern among elasmobranchs where sexual dimorphism in body size is linked to the energetic demands of egg case production. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild, estimated from tag-recapture and age-reading studies conducted at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], a longevity that permits multiple reproductive cycles over an individual's lifetime and contributes to population resilience under moderate fishing pressure.

First pupping in the blonde ray, determined through examination of the presence of fully formed egg cases in captive females, occurs at approximately 2,009 days after hatching [tR = approximately 2,009 days after hatching] at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], representing a considerable delay before the onset of breeding activity. This protracted juvenile period is energetically devoted to somatic growth, as individuals must attain a sufficiently large body size to accommodate the production of large, leathery egg cases and support the metabolic costs of repeated laying events. During this pre-reproductive phase, immature individuals forage actively on crustaceans and molluscs, gradually shifting their diet as they grow. The age at birth of approximately 213 days [ab = approximately 213 days] is brief compared to this extended maturation period, underscoring a life-history strategy where early development is rapid, but the transition to reproductive maturity is substantially delayed at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. Comparative data from related skates suggest that such a prolonged maturation window is associated with low natural mortality rates in adults, allowing a long reproductive lifespan to compensate for low annual fecundity.

Longevity data for the blonde ray, gathered from mark-recapture programmes and validated with vertebral ageing techniques at a consistent temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years], with the oldest individuals typically recorded among females, which also attain the largest body sizes. This lifespan, in conjunction with a first reproduction occurring at approximately 2,009 days after hatching [tR = approximately 2,009 days after hatching], results in a relatively brief reproductive window of perhaps 4 to 5 years during which a female can contribute offspring to the population at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. The total length at birth of 17 cm [Lb = 17 cm] represents approximately 14 percent of the ultimate length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], a proportional size that is comparable to other large rajiform skates. Given the low annual egg production, estimated at 30 eggs per year [Ri = 30 eggs per year], lifetime fecundity in this species is likely limited to approximately 120 to 150 eggs per female, placing substantial importance on the survival of each egg case and the successful emergence of viable neonates for population persistence.
